lede: Text columns are rarely in the shape a report needs: names to split, labels to build, ids with a number inside. Spark's string functions clean and reshape text on every row, and regular expressions handle the patterns plain functions can't.
objectives: Change case, trim spaces and measure text with `upper`, `lower`, `initcap`, `trim` and `length`
Join text with `concat` and `concat_ws`, and know how each treats a missing value
Find and replace patterns with `regexp_extract`, `regexp_replace` and `rlike`

blocks.md:
The shop's `customers`, `products` and `orders` are loaded as DataFrames with those names, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`.

Each string function takes a column (or a column name) and gives back a new column, worked out row by row. You use them inside `select`, like the arithmetic in lesson 9, and name the result with `alias`. `F.upper`, `F.lower` and `F.initcap` change the case, and `F.length` counts the characters.

blocks.title: Case and length
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

products.select(
    "name",
    F.upper("name").alias("shouting"),
    F.lower("name").alias("quiet"),
    F.length("name").alias("chars"),
).show(4)
blocks.note: The space and the hyphen count as characters, so `Pour-Over Kettle` is 16 long.

blocks.md: Text typed by people often has stray spaces and mixed case, so the same city can be written three ways. `F.trim` removes spaces at both ends (`ltrim` and `rtrim` do one end), and `F.initcap` writes each word with a capital first letter. Together they make the values match.

blocks.title: Tidy messy text
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

messy = spark.createDataFrame([("  Leeds ",), ("LEEDS",), ("leeds",)], "city STRING")
messy.select("city", F.length("city").alias("chars"), F.initcap(F.trim("city")).alias("clean")).show()
blocks.note: Functions nest: `trim` runs first, then `initcap` works on its result. All three rows end up as `Leeds`.

blocks.md:
To join text, `F.concat(a, b, ...)` puts the values side by side; a fixed piece of text needs `F.lit`. `F.concat_ws(sep, a, b, ...)` puts `sep` between them.

They differ on missing values: **`concat` gives a missing result if any part is missing**, while `concat_ws` just skips the missing parts.

blocks.title: Join text, with and without a missing part
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

people = spark.createDataFrame([("Ines", "Okafor"), ("Kofi", None)], "first STRING, last STRING")
people.select(
    F.concat("first", F.lit(" "), "last").alias("with_concat"),
    F.concat_ws(" ", "first", "last").alias("with_concat_ws"),
).show()
blocks.note: Kofi has no last name: `concat` gives `NULL`, `concat_ws` gives just `Kofi`. Pick the one whose behaviour you want.

blocks.md: `F.substring(col, pos, len)` takes `len` characters starting at position `pos`. Here positions start at **1**, not 0. `F.split(col, pattern)` cuts text into an array at every match of `pattern`, and you pick a piece with `[0]`, `[1]` and so on. Array positions start at **0**, so `[0]` is the first piece.

blocks.title: Cut text apart
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

customers.select(
    "name",
    F.split("name", " ")[0].alias("first"),
    F.split("name", " ")[1].alias("last"),
    F.substring("name", 1, 1).alias("initial"),
).show(3)
blocks.note: `split` makes `["Ines", "Okafor"]`, so `[0]` is the first name. `substring("name", 1, 1)` is the first character.

blocks.md:
A **regular expression** describes a pattern: `\d+` is one or more digits, `[^a-z0-9]+` is a run of characters that aren't lower-case letters or digits, `^` is the start and `$` the end. Write patterns as raw strings, `r"\d+"`, so Python leaves the backslashes alone.

- `F.regexp_extract(col, pattern, 0)` gives the part that matches (or `""` if nothing does). With a group in brackets, `1` gives the first group.
- `F.regexp_replace(col, pattern, new)` replaces every match.
- `F.col("x").rlike(pattern)` is a true or false column: true when the pattern is found somewhere in the text.

blocks.title: Patterns: extract, replace, test
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

orders.select("order_id", F.regexp_extract("order_id", r"\d+", 0).alias("number")).show(3)

products.select(
    "name",
    F.regexp_replace(F.lower("name"), r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-").alias("slug"),
    F.col("name").rlike(r"^(Camp|Trail) ").alias("outdoor_word"),
).show()
blocks.note: The number keeps its leading zeros because it's still text. In the slug, the space in `Chef Knife` and the hyphen and space in `Pour-Over Kettle` each become one `-`.

concept.prompt: `first` is `"Kofi"` and `last` is missing. What does `F.concat_ws(" ", "first", "last")` give?
concept.why: `concat_ws` skips missing parts. `concat` would give `NULL`, because one part is missing.
`substring` counts from 1, so position 2 is the first `0`, and it takes three characters: `001`.
Lower-case first, then replace each run of other characters with `-`. Without `lower`, the capitals would be replaced too.

review: String functions take a column and return a new one; use them in `select` with `alias`.
`upper`, `lower`, `initcap`, `trim` and `length` change case, remove outer spaces and count characters.
`concat` gives `NULL` if any part is missing; `concat_ws(sep, ...)` skips missing parts.
`substring(col, pos, len)` counts from 1. `split(col, pattern)` makes an array you index from 0.
`regexp_extract` pulls out a match (`""` if none), `regexp_replace` replaces every match and `rlike` tests for one.
Write regular expressions as raw strings: `r"\d+"`.
